analysis.one_liner: Blocks the FCC from regulating broadband internet unless it proves a market failure first.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after referral to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Communications subcommittee in early 2011, it sat without action until the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Communications Act to stop the Federal Communications Commission from setting any rules for internet access services unless the agency first formally proved a market failure, documented specific consumer harm, and showed the benefits of regulation outweigh the costs. It responds directly to the FCC's 2010 'Open Internet' rules, which barred broadband companies from blocking or slowing websites. In practice, the bill would have made the kind of network neutrality rules the FCC had just adopted extremely difficult, if not impossible, to sustain.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be the large cable and telephone companies that sell home internet service. They would be shielded from any FCC limits on how they manage, prioritize, or price traffic on their networks, giving them freedom to offer paid fast lanes, throttle heavy users' content, or favor their own services without a federal regulator stepping in.

how_it_helps.text: The FCC could not regulate rates, terms, conditions, provisioning, or use of internet access services unless it first transmitted a report to Congress concluding there is a market failure causing specific, identified consumer harm, and then completed a cost-benefit analysis showing regulation's benefits exceed its costs [S2] [S3].

Any regulation the FCC did adopt would have to be the least restrictive necessary, could not prohibit network management to address congestion or quality of service, and could not restrict measures to deter copyright infringement [S2] [S3].
Regulations would automatically sunset every two years unless the FCC re-proved that the market failure still existed and the regulation still passed a cost-benefit test [S3].

Enforcement would be complaint-driven only: a rule could be enforced against a company solely if the FCC, on a consumer's complaint, found the company violated the rule and caused that consumer specific and substantial harm [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary internet users. Without effective backstop rules, the companies that control home broadband could slow or prioritize traffic and charge websites for faster delivery, with consumers ultimately paying higher prices for content and getting whatever speed and access the provider decides to give them.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued in good faith that the bill imposed process discipline: the FCC would have to prove market failure, weigh investment and innovation effects, use the least restrictive means, and re-examine its rules every two years [S3].

The strongest objection is that the market-failure bar is so high it would function as a near-total ban on the FCC's authority over broadband: requiring proof that failures block 'a substantial number of consumers' from 'a substantial amount' of content before acting, and letting regulations lapse every two years, means rules could not keep pace with a market dominated by a few providers [S3].

Complaint-only enforcement shifts the burden to individual consumers to detect violations, file complaints, and prove specific, substantial harm — resources few households have against large internet providers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill framed itself as protecting investment and innovation by keeping regulators off broadband networks, and its process requirements are genuinely stricter than ordinary rulemaking. But the practical effect would be to remove the FCC's main tools for keeping broadband companies from controlling what users can access online, in a market where most households often have only one or two viable providers. The cost to everyday internet users outweighed the procedural benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology subcommittee, and it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cliff Stearns introduced the bill on January 5, 2011, the first day of the new 112th Congress [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on February 1, 2011 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology [S5] [S2].
Three Republican House members cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers did not get the statutory shield they would have gained had the bill passed, so the outcome left the FCC's existing authority over internet access intact. Everyday internet users were better off than they would have been under the bill.

for.name: Rep. Cliff Stearns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 5, 2011, the opening day of the 112th Congress

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, and no action advanced the bill after its February 2011 subcommittee referral [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have barred the FCC from regulating how they price, manage, or prioritize internet traffic unless the agency first proved a market failure, and complaint-only enforcement plus a two-year sunset would have made effective rules nearly impossible to sustain. Their gain would come at the expense of household internet users, in a market where most consumers have few if any alternative providers.

industries.industry: Internet content, application, and service companies
industries.note: Websites and streaming or application businesses rely on open access to users; without enforceable neutrality rules, broadband companies could charge them for priority delivery or slow their services, costs that would ultimately be passed to consumers.
